Every meaning of "interpolate" shares a single heartbeat: placing or estimating something in between existing things. Whether you're dealing with words, numbers, or data, the act of interpolating always involves filling a gap — slipping something into the middle of something else. Keep this image in your head: you have two points, and you are carefully inserting something between them.
Meaning 1: To Insert Something Into Text or Speech

In everyday language, to interpolate means to insert a word, a comment, a sentence, or a passage into something that already exists — a conversation, a piece of writing, a speech, a book.

Example:

The professor was mid-sentence when her student interpolated a question about the experiment.

Here, the student pushed a question into the middle of something that was already happening. The question wasn't at the beginning or end — it was inserted in between.

Another example:

The editor interpolated a paragraph into the article to provide more context.

The paragraph didn't exist in the original article. It was slipped in between existing content.

The subtle shade of meaning here: When scholars use this word about old texts — ancient manuscripts, religious books, historical documents — it often carries a slightly suspicious tone. It implies that someone, at some point after the original was written, secretly inserted material that wasn't originally there. It can suggest tampering.

Historians believe certain passages in that medieval chronicle were interpolated by monks who wanted to change its meaning.

So when applied to texts, "interpolate" can mean anything from innocent editing to deliberate alteration.
Meaning 2: To Estimate a Value That Falls Between Two Known Values (Math & Science)

This is the most precise, technical meaning of the word, and it's used constantly in mathematics, science, statistics, engineering, and computing.

The setup: You have two known data points — a value at Point A and a value at Point B. You want to figure out what the value probably was at some point between A and B. That process of reasoned estimation is called interpolation.

A simple example:

On Monday, a plant was 10 cm tall. On Friday, it was 20 cm tall. By interpolating, we can estimate it was probably around 15 cm tall on Wednesday.

You didn't measure it on Wednesday. But because Wednesday sits between Monday and Friday, and you know the values at both ends, you can make a logical, mathematically grounded estimate for the middle.

Another example:

The temperature sensor recorded 60°F at 9 AM and 80°F at 11 AM. The scientist interpolated to estimate the temperature at 10 AM was approximately 70°F.

Again: two known values, one unknown value sitting in between, and a calculation to estimate it.

This works best when the change between the two known points is smooth and consistent (like temperature rising gradually, or a plant growing steadily). The more irregular the pattern between the points, the less reliable the interpolation.
The Most Important Contrast: Interpolate vs. Extrapolate

These two words are brothers, and confusing them is one of the most common mistakes people make. Once you understand the difference, it's unforgettable.

  • Interpolate = estimate a value that falls within the range of what you already know.
  • Extrapolate = estimate a value that falls beyond the range of what you already know.

Using the plant example:

  • You know the height on Monday (10 cm) and Friday (20 cm).
  • Estimating Wednesday's height → Interpolation (Wednesday is between Monday and Friday).
  • Estimating next Monday's height → Extrapolation (next Monday is beyond your data).

Interpolation is generally considered more reliable because you're working within a confirmed, bounded range. Extrapolation is riskier because you're venturing into unknown territory past your data.

In the digital world, "interpolate" is used constantly — especially in video, animation, and image editing.

When a video is recorded at 30 frames per second and software needs to display it at 60 frames per second, it has to create new frames. How? It looks at the existing frame before and after the missing one, and calculates what a frame in between them should look like. That's interpolation.

When a digital photo is enlarged and new pixels need to be created between existing pixels to fill the bigger image, the software interpolates — it estimates what color those in-between pixels should be based on their neighbors.

The word means exactly the same thing it always does: figuring out or creating what belongs in between.

Since you'll encounter this word in different forms:

  • Interpolation (noun) — the act of interpolating, or the thing inserted. "The interpolation of that comment changed the tone of the speech."
  • Interpolated (adjective / past tense) — something that has been inserted or estimated. "That was an interpolated passage, not part of the original text."
  • Interpolating (present participle) — currently doing the act. "The software is interpolating the missing frames."
  • Interpolator (noun) — a person or tool that interpolates.
The Full Picture in Plain Terms

To interpolate is to fill in the middle. Whether you're inserting a comment into a conversation, adding a sentence into a book, estimating a temperature between two readings, or having software generate a missing video frame — you are always working between two existing points. The gap is the target. The thing you place or calculate is the interpolation.

If someone says "we interpolated the data," they calculated reasonable estimates for the missing values that fall within the data they had. If someone says "a line was interpolated into the manuscript," someone inserted a sentence into an existing text — and the word quietly hints that this may not have been the original author's doing.

The word always implies a kind of careful, reasoned insertion into the space between.
